item.title: Neuropathologic Correlates of Cognitive Decline in Community-Dwelling Elders Who Die as Centenarians.
item.description:
Neurology
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Brain pathologies are common in the elderly; however, their contribution to Alzheimer dementia risk and cognitive decline in those who die as centenarians remain unclear. This study examines the frequency of Alzheimer disease neuropathologic changes (ADNC), limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy neuropathologic change (LATE-NC), and other brain pathologies and their association with Alzheimer dementia risk and cognitive decline in centenarians. METHODS: This clinicopathologic study included older participants from the Religious Orders Study and Rush Memory and Aging Project, 2 ongoing clinicopathologic cohort studies of aging and dementia, who underwent annual clinical evaluations and autopsy. Participants were evaluated annually for cognitive status and followed for a mean (SD) of 11.4 (5.3) years before death. Neuropathologic evaluation included ADNC (and separately β-amyloid load and tangle density), LATE-NC, presence or absence of neocortical Lewy bodies (LBs), hippocampal sclerosis of aging (HS-A), primary age-related tauopathy (PART), and 5 cerebrovascular disease (CVD) pathologies including arteriolosclerosis, atherosclerosis, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, macroinfarcts, and microinfarcts. Multivariable regression and linear mixed-effects models were applied. RESULTS: A total of 104 centenarians were included in this study. The mean (SD) age at death was 102 (1.9) years, 84% were female, 58% had Alzheimer dementia, 21% had mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and 21% had no cognitive impairment (NCI). All 3 clinical diagnostic groups exhibited pathologies, including any type of CVD (94%), ADNC (72%; 73% of them were intermediate and 27% of them were high), LATE-NC (58%, 30% of them exhibiting HS-A), HS-A (18%, 95% had LATE-NC), PART (28%), and neocortical LBs (11%). Mixed pathologies, particularly ADNC + LATE-NC + CVD, were common in the Alzheimer dementia group (52%) compared with NCI (36%) and MCI (23%). After adjusted for age at death, sex, education, and other brain pathologies, only LATE-NC and tangles (specifically intermediate/high ADNC with Braak stage V) were associated with more rapid decline in global cognition and increased odds of Alzheimer dementia. DISCUSSION: Brain pathology, but not dementia, is nearly inevitable in those who die as centenarians. LATE-NC and tangles are the key contributors to cognitive decline. Future study investigating resilience factors may inform preventive strategies.

item.title: Poorer inhibition and switching are associated with lower white matter fibre density in the superior longitudinal fasciculus in groups clinically at-risk of probable Alzheimer's disease dementia.
item.description:
Journal of neurology
Executive dysfunction and white matter microstructural alterations in the superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) may occur in the clinically defined at-risk groups of Alzheimer's disease (AD) dementia and be potentially useful and early markers of risk. We used diffusion-weighted MRI and fixel-based analysis to investigate inhibition/switching executive functioning and white matter properties of three SLF subdivisions (SLF 1, SLF 2, SLF 3) in groups clinically at-risk of AD-dementia: controls (C; n = 35), subjective cognitive decline (SCD; n = 60), single-domain amnestic mild cognitive impairment (aMCI; n = 55), and multiple-domain amnestic MCI (mMCI; n = 52). Individuals with probable AD-dementia (n = 27) were also compared with controls. Linear trend analyses showed increasingly poorer executive functioning performance and lower fibre density (FD) in the right SLF 2 and bilateral SLF 3 across groups. Analysis of covariance (age, sex) revealed SCD and mMCI groups had lower FD bilaterally in the SLF 3 than controls. The AD-dementia group showed more extensively reduced FD in four of the six SLF divisions, and lower fibre density cross-section (FDC) in five of the six SLF divisions than controls. Partial least-squares (PLS) analyses showed that poorer executive functioning, but not processing speed, was associated with lower FD in the SLF in the at-risk sample. This pattern was also found in AD-dementia/controls PLS, which additionally showed this association with FDC. Collectively, our results implicate altered microstructural fibre properties in the SLF and poorer executive functioning in groups at risk of AD-dementia, with FD changes in SLF present in SCD, prior to objective cognitive decline.

item.title: Linguistic contextualization in the human hippocampus.
item.description:
Nature human behaviour
Word meanings in language are contextualized by surrounding words. Inspired by the self-attention mechanism in transformer-based large language models (LLMs), we hypothesized that structural composition in the brain arises from combining canonical (non-contextual) word representations with those of nearby words. We analysed single unit activity in the human hippocampus, a region involved in semantic and contextual processing, while n = 10 participants listened to podcasts. We found that hippocampal neurons encoded word position within a clause, using both ordinal and frequency-domain positional encoding. Moreover, neural responses to specific words reflected both the lexical semantics of the word and a weighted sum of the embeddings of preceding words. The relative weighting of these contextualizing words correlated with LLM self-attention weights. These findings suggest that contextualization in the brain makes use of vectorial shifts that have a resemblance to attentional reweighting in LLMs, and highlight the role of the mesial temporal lobe within the broader language network.

item.title: Spatiotemporal brain dynamics of limb ownership perception.
item.description:
Nature communications
We experience our limbs as our own, but how does the brain generate this fundamental sense of body ownership? Previous studies have relied mainly on fMRI or lesion mapping, providing a static view of the neural mechanisms underlying body ownership. Using magnetoencephalography, robotically controlled visuotactile stimulation, and multivariate analysis across the rubber hand illusion, a real hand condition, and multiple control conditions, we identified source vector dissimilarity patterns reflecting ownership of the left arm. Three phases of ownership-specific activity patterns emerged: (i) anticipatory patterns in medial frontal cortex, right posterior parietal cortex, and right posterior cerebellum before tactile stimulation; (ii) multisensory integration patterns in right dorsal and ventral premotor cortex, right posterior parietal cortex, and anterior cerebellum at 116-156 ms poststimulus; and (iii) later bilateral insular and left hemisphere patterns at 184-232 ms. These findings provide a whole-brain, time-resolved map of activity patterns underlying body ownership, revealing its dynamic neural construction.

item.title: Network Control Theory in Psychiatry: From Connectivity-Derived Controllability to Brain-State Transitions and Interventions.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Psychiatric disorders are increasingly conceptualized as disruptions in brain dynamics, particularly in how activity patterns evolve over time. Network Control Theory (NCT), a framework derived from control engineering, has emerged as a promising approach for studying these dynamics. Yet, despite its growing application in psychiatry, it remains unclear whether NCT has provided mechanistic or clinical insights beyond conventional measures of network topology. Here, we conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review of NCT applications across major psychiatric disorders in adults. Of 178 records identified, 26 studies met inclusion criteria, representing 17 unique cohorts spanning schizophrenia spectrum disorders, major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Across studies, a recurring pattern of lower modal controllability was reported in several disorders (3 independent cohorts), although regional findings were heterogeneous and diagnostic specificity was limited. In contrast, task-based analyses under cognitive load (2 cohorts) and energy-based metrics (2 cohorts), though scarce, revealed more extensive case-control abnormalities and between-disorder differentiation. Intervention studies provided preliminary evidence that NCT-derived measures may predict treatment response and inform individualized neuromodulation targets (4 cohorts). However, 21 of 26 studies exclusively relied on connectivity-derived controllability metrics that were closely related to conventional measures of network topology and characterized model-implied control properties rather than directly observed state transitions. Furthermore, translational evidence came largely from single-arm, retrospective and simulation studies. The distinct value of NCT in psychiatry therefore remains to be established. Future progress requires the use of empirically observed brain states, energy-based measures, and prospective intervention studies.

item.title: Motor pre-selection modulates action observation effects in sensorimotor cortices: a MEG study.
item.description:
NeuroImage
According to the Motor Simulation theory, observing an action automatically activates matching motor representations. This can explain why, in automatic imitation tasks, responses are faster when the observed action matches the required one, compared to when it differs. However, the automatic imitation task setting represents a very peculiar situation where participants need to pre-select the motor representations corresponding to the actions that they might observe, a situation quite different from daily-life contexts such as sports (e.g., tennis or basketball) where actions pre-selected for output are typically different from those observed, and where imitation errors or tendencies are seldom observed. This leads to the following question: Does the motor cortex response to observed actions depend on whether they match the motor representations pre-selected for output? In the present magnetoencephalography experiment, we studied, within the hand-related primary sensorimotor cortex, the oscillatory dynamics produced by the observation of hand actions in two conditions: either while participants pre-selected motor representations similar to those observed, or while they pre-selected markedly different motor representations, such as those involved in feet actions. Our data show that the motor cortex reacts differently to action observation in the two pre-selection conditions: alpha- and beta-band activity showed stronger desynchronization when the pre-selection involved motor representations matching those observed compared to non-matching ones. Specifically, observing hand actions while pre-selecting non-matching feet movements elicited a late rebound-like increase in alpha- and beta-band activity that was not observed when hand actions were pre-selected.

item.title: Explainable multi-group dynamic causal distribution learning framework to disentangle common and specific dynamic effective connectivity across MCI stages.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Brain functional networks exhibit an intrinsic architecture that is preserved across brain disorder groups, upon which different groups display distinct patterns of abnormal interactions. Exploring the common and specific network patterns is crucial for revealing common pathological mechanisms, group-specific alterations, and disease progression. Dynamic effective connectivity (dEC) characterizes time-varying causal interactions among brain regions and provides an effective means of investigating common and specific network patterns. However, the disentangled learning of common and specific dEC across multiple groups remains underexplored, limiting a systematic understanding of dynamic causal mechanisms in brain networks across disorders and disease stages. We propose an explainable multi-group dynamic causal distribution learning framework that integrates spatial and temporal information to identify common and specific dEC distributions among different groups. Experiments on synthetic datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively and robustly identifies causality and disentangles common and specific causal structures. When applied to real-world data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, the proposed framework uncovers common and specific dEC across mild cognitive impairment (MCI) stages. Results show that, as MCI worsens, the dEC within the visual network and among functional hubs of the default mode network remain stable, whereas dEC associated with episodic memory, emotional processing, and interoception shift from compensatory to decompensatory patterns. The code is available at https://github.com/OrangeLY-byte/EMGDCD.

item.title: Cognitive control networks in human and macaque.
item.description:
eLife
A much-replicated finding in human brain imaging is a distributed 'multiple-demand' or MD system, increasing in activity for many kinds of cognitive demand, and centrally involved in cognitive control. MD regions are proposed to encode a distributed mental model of critical task events, bound together in the roles and relationships needed to direct action selection. Though previous data hint at a corresponding network in the macaque, there has been no direct comparison to human data. Here we used functional magnetic resonance imaging to measure whole-brain activation in a multi-step saccadic maze task, compared to a control requiring similar moves but without goal-based decisions. Human data were a close match to the canonical MD network, extended to include adjacent regions, and in particular much of the canonical dorsal attention network. Data from two monkeys suggested correspondences in dorsomedial frontal, insula/orbitofrontal, and posterior temporal cortex. In lateral frontal cortex, there was just a single, largely dorsal activation patch, in contrast to multiple distinct human patches. In one animal, as in humans, there was accompanying activation of dorsal and medial parietal cortex. In macaques, as in humans, together with previous data, our findings suggest an extended and strongly interconnected brain network recruited by increased cognitive challenge.

item.title: Ramping-up hippocampal ripples and their neocortical coupling support human visual short-term memory.
item.description:
eLife
Emerging evidence suggests that the hippocampus contributes to visual short-term memory (VSTM). However, the neural mechanisms through which hippocampal activity supports the maintenance of VSTM representations remain largely unknown. Here, using intracranial EEG recordings from human participants performing a delayed match-to-sample task for naturalistic objects, we investigated the role of hippocampal ripple activity-brief high-frequency oscillations associated with memory replay-in VSTM maintenance and hippocampal-neocortical communication. We found that hippocampal ripple rates progressively ramped up during the maintenance period and supported successful VSTM. More critically, hippocampal ripples were temporally coupled with the ripples in the lateral temporal lobe (LTL), and these coupled ripples were associated with memory reactivation in the LTL. These findings provide direct evidence that hippocampal-neocortical interaction via coupled ripples supports VSTM, extending the role of hippocampal ripples from long-term consolidation to short-term mnemonic processes and offering new insights into the dynamic coding mechanisms of working memory.

item.title: MAMBAxBrain: A multi-task neural framework linking brain functional dynamics to individual fingerprints, cognitive and disease states.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) contains rich individual, cognitive, and pathological information, yet no universal model exists for multi-task modeling of these dimensions. Here, we introduce MAMBAxBrain, a multi-task neural framework that integrates Mamba architecture with functional connectivity analysis to jointly model the temporal dynamics and spatial coordination of neural activity. MAMBAxBrain achieves high accuracy across four distinct fMRI objectives, including brain fingerprinting, cognitive task decoding, reaction time prediction, and schizophrenia classification, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art methods with robust cross-session generalization. Interpretability analyses show that each task engages distinct, biologically plausible circuitry: from higher-order association cortex for identity to subcortical-motor loops for reaction time and disrupted control-sensory connectivity for schizophrenia. These findings inform a longstanding debate: rather than operating through wholly separate or entirely shared systems, the brain preferentially recruits task-specific circuits while retaining common representational structure across functions.

item.title: Cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) binds talin and is anchored at the postsynaptic density by direct PDZ interactions.
item.description:
Science advances
Cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) is a serine/threonine kinase essential for brain development and function. Mutations in CDKL5 cause CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD), a severe early-onset epileptic encephalopathy associated with impaired synapse formation and function. However, how CDKL5 mutations disrupt synaptic function remains unclear. Here, we show that the major neuronal isoform of CDKL5 contains a C-terminal PDZ domain-binding motif that mediates direct binding to PSD-95 and SHANK PDZ domains and recruits CDKL5 to the postsynaptic density. Disrupting this motif mislocalized CDKL5, reduced dendritic spine density, and impaired spine maturation. We also show that the CDKL5 kinase domain binds the R8 rod domain of the mechanosensitive scaffold talin. Mutation of the talin-binding interface or reduced cellular contractility altered CDKL5 positioning relative to focal adhesions. These findings define how CDKL5 is targeted to synapses, suggest that talin mechanoswitching may position CDKL5 kinase activity, and highlight the importance of C-terminal anchoring for interpreting pathogenic truncations.

item.title: Attention increases the spread of modality-invariant information across the cortex.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Attention shapes our perception by allowing us to focus on relevant stimuli that are selected for conscious processing. In this work we assessed to what degree attention influences the extraction of modality-invariant information, that is, information that is independent of the input stimulus modality. To this end, we analyze fMRI data of subjects viewing naturalistic images and reading short textual descriptions while paying attention to only one of the two modalities. Using cross-modality decoding, we found modality-invariant representations in a small area of the cortex even in the absence of attention, spreading to much larger regions when stimuli are attended. This work demonstrates how state-of-the-art decoding techniques on large-scale data can be used to expand our knowledge on how attention shapes specific high-level representations in the brain.

item.title: Shared and distinct neural pathways of aversive and appetitive pain-related learning.
item.description:
Communications biology
Aversive and appetitive learning are central to adaptive behaviour, and pain and avoidance are powerful examples of such forces shaping human behaviour. Alterations in learning are thought to contribute to the development and maintenance of chronic pain, yet their neural underpinnings remain unclear. In this registered within-subject fMRI study (German Clinical Trials Register, DRKS-ID: DRKS00027448), we examined both aversive and appetitive pain learning during acquisition and extinction in 68 healthy individuals. Ratings confirm successful learning, with exploratory analyses suggesting stronger aversive acquisition and incomplete extinction. Both conditions engage the visual cortex during acquisition, with increased connectivity to the right operculum. Aversive acquisition further elicits stronger mediodorsal thalamus activity and heightened connectivity with the locus coeruleus, alongside sustained parahippocampal activation during extinction. Incomplete aversive extinction is linked to ongoing visual cortex activity during pain anticipation. Findings suggest shared neural substrates, but stronger aversive recruitment of rapid encoding and persistent memory systems.
