item.title: Mismatch Negativity and General Cognitive Ability - A Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Intelligence or general cognitive ability (GCA) is fundamental to human behavior and cognition. It impacts important life outcomes like educational success, and even health and longevity have been related to differences in GCA. Understanding the biological basis of such individual variations presents a crucial goal of neuroscience. The mismatch negativity (MMN) is an event-related brain potential that can be measured when-within a series of frequent standard stimuli, rare deviants are presented-and is suggested to reflect conscious (active) or unconscious (passive) detection processes of the brain. Importantly, variations in MMN amplitude and latency have been linked to differences in GCA. Yet findings vary considerably. This preregistered meta-analysis provides a comprehensive and structured overview of the current state of research. Following the study selection process in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines, and the rating of study design quality with the Study Design and Implementation Assessment Device for Individual Difference Research (DIAD-ID), the association between GCA and MMN amplitude and latency was examined in 645 healthy adults across 12 included studies. The estimated across-sample associations between MMN and GCA were small, but significant (MMN amplitude-GCA: r = -0.09, MMN latency-GCA: r = -0.16; p < 0.01) and moderators were identified. Between-sample heterogeneity was moderate, with no evidence of publication bias. Our findings suggest that higher cognitive ability is associated with slightly stronger and faster MMN responses. However, the low estimated across-sample effect sizes and the small number of included studies also highlight the need for more research.

item.title: Where could the brain keep a symbol?
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Neuroscience routinely describes memories as stored neural symbols, yet durable memory and successful retrieval do not establish a separately accessible symbolic vehicle. I distinguish retention, the claim that a physical change persists and later influences behavior, from symbolic storage, the stronger computational claim that a description can be accessed independently of the operation it specifies. The criterion is functional and system-relative and does not rule out neural activity as access. It requires specifying, before testing, the candidate vehicle, its proposed use, the system boundary, and an endogenous route reaching the vehicle without using it. DNA meets the criterion: replication preserves nucleotide sequence without producing the encoded gene product. Evidence from synapses and circuits establishes persistent, functionally useful organization but has not shown this separation for any neural memory vehicle; in these states, identified reads are executions that modify what they read. Hippocampal replay, neuromodulation, and artificial-network checkpoints show that the verdict depends on the vehicle and operations compared. I agree with Gallistel that intracellular nucleic acid mechanisms could provide a genuine store, but disagree that behavioral precision alone requires one. Maintained coupling, in which memory is sustained by continual recalibration rather than read from a store, offers an alternative whose predictions depend on error source: drift can be corrected where a reference signal remains, but a unique, never-revisited episode offers none. Current evidence favors retention without symbolic storage in synapses and circuits; I propose operational tests that could overturn this verdict. Either way, retention and use remain memory.

item.title: Perceptual glimpses are locally accumulated and globally maintained at distinct processing levels.
item.description:
eLife
Making decisions often requires the integration of multiple pieces of information. An extensive body of research has investigated the neural architecture underpinning evidence accumulation in perceptual tasks where information is continuously present, but less is known about how this neural architecture operates in situations affording only intermittent glimpses of an evidence source. In two electroencephalography experiments, human participants judged the direction of up to two pulses of motion evidence separated by gaps of varying duration. Our behavioural analysis found that participants used both pulses but underutilised the second and showed no systematic decrease in accuracy as a function of gap duration. At the neural level, motor beta lateralisation tracked cumulative evidence across pulses, maintaining a sustained representation of the decision variable through the gap and until response. In contrast, the centroparietal positivity (CPP), a previously characterised signature of evidence accumulation, built up transiently to a peak that scaled with each pulse's contribution to the decision variable (i.e. the absolute belief update it produced), falling back to baseline in between pulses. These patterns were recapitulated in a model where pulse-information transiently integrated at the CPP level is fed to and maintained at a bounded motor level. In this model, the evidence in the second pulse is only integrated to the extent that the evidence in the first pulse falls short of the bound, or not integrated at all if a bound has already been hit.

item.title: Aperiodic EEG Activity Is a Domain-Specific Marker of Attentional Aging in Neurotypical Adults.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Aperiodic neural activity has been reliably shown to be reduced among older adults, and these reductions are associated with age-related cognitive decline. These results suggest that aperiodic activity, as measured by the spectral exponent, might be a viable electrophysiological biomarker for cognitive aging. However, this has not been tested longitudinally, within participants, during normal aging. Here, we used a longitudinal cohort of either sex to test whether changes in aperiodic activity between two sessions, ∼5 years apart, track behavioral change across two domains: sustained attention (Psychomotor Vigilance Test) and executive function (modified Simon task). We found that aperiodic activity declined within individuals after the interval, independent of age at baseline. This within-person change tracked concurrent changes in reaction times during sustained attention but was not associated with changes in any Simon task measure. Within a resampling framework, the aperiodic-PVT association was stable across cohort resamples and independently fitted partitions, though it was not confirmed in a small, frozen held-out set. These findings suggest the longitudinal decline in aperiodic activity tracks attentional processing speed rather than executive function, supporting its potential as a domain-specific biomarker of attentional aging in neurotypical populations.

item.title: Probing the Neural Geometry of Conscious Object Perception in Time.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Conscious object recognition is a critical brain function, key to making sense of the plethora of visual inputs and guiding adaptive behavior. Yet, the sequence of neural processing underlying conscious object recognition remains unclear. Existing proposals alternatively suggest that conscious object recognition proceeds in a "coarse-to-fine" sequence or a "fine-to-coarse" sequence. Here, we recorded high-density EEG while participants of both sexes performed a threshold-level object recognition task under different viewing conditions. Both superordinate and basic-level category information emerged early in neural activity, followed by a late superordinate category representation in an abstract format that is disentangled from low-level object features. Strikingly, in the early period, while basic-level category information positively correlated with perceptual awareness, superordinate category information negatively predicted perceptual awareness. In contrast, both superordinate and basic-level category information positively correlated with objective categorization accuracy in the early period. In the late period, both levels of category information positively correlated with awareness. These results suggest that neural processing underlying conscious object perception proceeds from the basic to the superordinate category level.

item.title: Perception of Tones versus Tone Streams under Random Multi-tone Masking and Its Representation in Auditory Cortex.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
When repeated tones are presented among random masker tones, their perceptual organization is often variable. In some trials, they cannot be segregated from the masker tones. In other trials, often with a delay, they form coherent streams, segregated from the masker tones. A strong awareness-related negativity is evoked by each segregated tone of the stream in auditory cortex. A similar negative-going response has been observed when subtle, isolated tones are detected versus missed, raising the question of whether target tones that do not form a stream under informational masking are still perceived or not. Here a paradigm is introduced to probe this question while activity in auditory cortex was recorded with magnetoencephalography. Human listeners (13 female, 8 male) were instructed to indicate when they detected an isochronous stream of tones under multi-tone masking while listening to the stimulus. Thereafter, they indicated if a cue tone, presented subsequently to each trial, was comprised in the target and masker combination. Results confirmed that target tones could still be perceived in the subset of trials where they did not form a coherent stream, but the detectability in the cued frequency report was higher for tones forming a stream. A prominent awareness-related negativity was only observed when the tones formed a stream, suggesting that this response reflects the perceptual organization of the tones into streams and beyond the pure perception of the tones themselves. We speculate that the perceptual organization into a stream further enhances the detectability of the tones comprised in the stream.

item.title: Representation of Emotional Expressions across the Face and Voice Brain Networks.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Recognizing emotions from faces and voices is fundamental to successful social interaction, yet how the brain represents emotional information across sensory systems remains unclear. Here, we systematically mapped the contribution of individually defined face- and voice-selective cortical regions in 24 human participants of either sex to unimodal and crossmodal emotion expressions. Using multivariate pattern classification, we show that emotional expressions are robustly decodable from the dominant sensory modality across all individually defined face- and voice-selective areas and that these representations cannot be accounted for by low- and mid-level stimulus properties alone. Strikingly, emotional information from the nondominant modality-vocal expressions within face networks and facial expressions within voice networks-was also represented throughout the network, with the exception of the occipital face areas. Crossmodal decoding further revealed a shared neural code for facial and vocal emotions in the temporal voice areas, posterior superior temporal sulcus, and precentral gyrus, indicating that these regions contain emotion representations that generalize across sensory modalities. Furthermore, in most face- and voice-selective regions, audiovisual emotional expressions could be distinguished from representations elicited by the dominant unimodal modality, indicating that bimodal signals are not simply represented as their strongest sensory component. Together, these findings reveal that emotion representations are distributed broadly across face- and voice-selective regions and identify temporofrontal regions as key sites supporting modality-independent emotion representations.

item.title: Neuropathologic Correlates of Cognitive Functions in Patients With Essential Tremor Without Dementia: Beyond the Cerebellum.
item.description:
Neurology
Background and objectives Essential tremor (ET) is characterized not only by motor disturbances but also, in many cases, by a wide array of cognitive symptoms. Accumulating evidence implicates pathways beyond the cerebellum by which cognitive changes emerge. However, the extracerebellar neuropathologic correlates of specific cognitive symptoms have not been examined. This study evaluated these potential clinicopathologic associations in older adults with ET. Methods Participants were adults ≥55 years with ET who were followed prospectively and longitudinally and donated their brains for neuropathologic evaluation as part of the Clinical-Pathological Study of Cognitive Impairment in Essential Tremor study. Cognitive outcomes included attention, executive function, language, memory, and visuospatial function. Postmortem neuropathologic assessment included Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer's Disease (CERAD) neuritic plaque scores, Thal β-amyloid A score, Braak and Braak neurofibrillary tangle (NFT) stage, and Braak Lewy pathology stage. Regional cerebral cortical atrophy ratings (neocortical and hippocampal), cerebral amyloid angiopathy, and markers of cerebrovascular health were also rated. Regression models examined neuropathologic correlates of cognitive function, adjusting for numerous confounders. Sensitivity analyses examined robustness of findings. Results The sample consisted of 57 individuals with ET and without dementia (mean age = 88.6 ± 5.4 years; 54.4% female, 71.9% cognitively normal, 28.1% with mild cognitive impairment). Higher amyloid burden was associated with lower attention (CERAD β = -0.48, p < 0.001; Thal β = -0.37, p < 0.01) and lower executive function (CERAD β = -0.40, p 0.01; Thal β = -0.33, p = 0.01). CERAD score was associated with lower language (β = -0.31, p = 0.04). Braak NFT stage was associated with lower attention (β = -0.26, p = 0.04) and lower executive function (β = -0.28, p = 0.03). Hippocampal atrophy was associated with lower memory performance (β = -0.29, p = 0.04). Discussion Core pathologies of AD, amyloid and tau, are associated with decrements in attention and executive function in older adults with ET and without dementia, while hippocampal atrophy is associated with lower memory performance. These results, consistent with a growing literature on extracerebellar pathologies in ET, suggest that multidomain cognitive symptoms among older adults with ET and without dementia may be driven in large part by AD-related cortical degenerative processes. Ongoing work is examining the molecular basis of these processes. Limitations include a highly educated, demographically homogeneous, and relatively small sample, as well as a lack of a control group.

item.title: Distinct Amygdala-Frontopolar and Amygdala-Medial Temporal Pathways Support Temporal Memory for Emotional Events.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Growing evidence suggests that emotion shapes temporal aspects of memory-such as remembering when an event occurred-yet the neural bases of these effects remain unclear. Prior work indicates that temporal context representations in memory are supported by the functions of the medial temporal lobe (MTL) and prefrontal regions, including hippocampus, perirhinal cortex, and lateral frontopolar cortex (FPl). These regions have privileged access to amygdala-originated affective signals that may mediate emotional influences on temporal memory. To test whether these candidate pathways shape temporal memory for emotional events, participants encoded trial-unique negative and positive images in the scanner, followed by a surprise temporal memory task. We found that more negative stimuli were associated with greater amygdala activation and lower temporal memory error for when emotional images occurred. Replicating and extending prior work, higher stimulus-evoked multivoxel pattern similarity in the hippocampus and FPl was associated with higher temporal memory error. Notably, greater amygdala responding to emotional images predicted higher between-trial pattern similarity in the hippocampus but lower within- and between-trial similarity in FPl. Amygdala engagement was also correlated with greater perirhinal activation, which in turn predicted stronger item memory and a recency bias in temporal memory estimates. Collectively, these findings reveal distinct-and opposing-modulatory effects of amygdala-FPl and amygdala-MTL pathways on temporal memory, with the potential to sharpen and blur memory for when emotional events occurred.

item.title: Cross-domain encoding models reveal shared and domain-specific neural representations across language and mathematics.
item.description:
Science advances
Whether language and mathematics rely on shared or distinct neural representations remains unresolved in cognitive neuroscience. Here, we combined latent features from a large language model with functional magnetic resonance imaging encoding models to test cross-domain generalization in 32 participants performing sentence comprehension and calculation tasks. Cross-domain prediction identified cortical regions showing partially shared representations, most consistently in the left area 55b, while control analyses suggested that these effects could not be fully explained by low-level visual or task-general factors. Domain-specificity contrasts revealed stronger language-related prediction in the left superior temporal sulcus and angular gyrus and math-related prediction in the left precentral sulcus and bilateral intraparietal sulci. Model-weight analyses revealed distinct weight profiles associated with shared and domain-specific prediction patterns. Cross-domain regions also exhibited task-dependent functional coupling with language- and math-related networks. Together, these findings suggest that language and mathematics involve partially shared neural representations alongside domain-specific cortical organization, helping reconcile previous contrasting views on their neural basis.

item.title: Auditory cortical coding of spectrotemporal modulations is sufficient to support perceptual categorization of speech and music.
item.description:
Science advances
Auditory processing is typically described as hierarchical, culminating in neural representation of abstract categories. However, it remains unclear whether category-selective responses in auditory cortex require representational mechanisms beyond the coding of acoustic features or whether the acoustic representations already available in the auditory cortex are sufficient to account for categorization. Here, we test whether cortical coding of spectrotemporal modulation (STM) features is sufficient to support speech-music categorization by combining human intracranial recordings with continuous behavioral judgments of a naturalistic soundtrack in which speech and music occur both separately and simultaneously. We show that temporal and spectral modulation patterns largely characterize speech and music, respectively, and that cortical auditory regions robustly track these features over time, with distinct oscillatory frequency bands preferentially encoding temporal and spectral modulations. Critically, cortical representations of STMs predicted perceptual categorical judgments gathered in an independent sample. Last, speech- and music-related STM representations showed stronger tracking of category-specific acoustical features in left versus right cortical auditory regions, respectively. These findings indicate that the efficient neural coding of acoustical features provides a sufficient basis for the categorical distinction between speech and music and that the temporal and spectral components of this representation are implemented through distinct oscillatory mechanisms.

item.title: The hippocampus as a latent diffusion engine for memory, perception and cognitive dysfunction.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
The hippocampus is a central cognitive hub whose dysfunction contributes to most neurodegenerative dementias. Despite extensive knowledge of its anatomy, physiology and circuitry, a unifying account that links hippocampal dynamics to cognition and clinical syndromes remains lacking. Drawing on systems neuroscience and recent advances in generative artificial intelligence, we conceptualize the hippocampus as a latent diffusion engine that compresses sensory, interoceptive and cognitive inputs into low-dimensional representations and regenerates percepts, episodic memories and imagined scenes for cortical integration. Travelling waves of cortico-hippocampal oscillations, aligned with large-scale functional gradients, schedule and structure this generative process and organize distributed neural activity into coherent, semantically grounded constructs. We formalize this proposal as stochastic latent oscillatory diffusion (SLOD), a biologically grounded framework that maps hippocampal-cortical computations onto specific anatomical substrates and dynamical processes. While we do not suggest that the hippocampus implements diffusion algorithms per se, we show that its computations can be decomposed into homologous operations including compression, stochastic exploration, conditioning and reconstruction, whose formal structure closely parallels that of latent diffusion models. Finally, we demonstrate how major neurodegenerative dementias, including the Alzheimer's disease spectrum, dementia with Lewy bodies and frontotemporal dementia, can be understood as selective breakdowns of distinct components of this generative architecture.

item.title: Remodeling stress-responsive networks following early life adversity: Insights from preclinical models.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Early life adversity (ELA) is a leading risk factor for the development of mental illness worldwide. While the association between experiencing developmental stress and psychopathology is robust, the underlying brain mechanisms remain unclear. Evidence from clinical and preclinical studies suggests that ELA may hijack typical developmental plasticity mechanisms, leading to maladaptive functional network changes. Understanding the nature and magnitude of these changes is complicated by several key dimensions, including the timing, type, and severity of ELA, as well as biological factors such as sex and genetic makeup. Preclinical models using primates and rodents have allowed for fine control over these variables, providing substantial evidence of pathways and related biomarkers impacted by ELA. The present review aims to bridge findings from human clinical data with preclinical research, highlighting well-supported ELA-induced changes in the functional connectivity of stress-sensitive pathways, as well as alterations in additional cortical and subcortical pathways which are susceptible to disturbances during development. We also present key neuromodulatory mechanisms contributing to connectivity changes observed in preclinical models, and sex-specific nuances. Addressing these critical gaps could enhance the potential of connectivity-based therapeutic approaches. Lastly, we consider the translatability of functional connectivity analyses using various preclinical techniques for studying the influence of ELA on the developing brain.

item.title: Hierarchical neural circuit theory of normalization and inter-areal communication.
item.description:
eLife
The primate brain exhibits a hierarchical, modular architecture with conserved microcircuits executing canonical computations across reciprocally connected cortical areas. We present a hierarchical neural circuit theory with feedback connections that dynamically implements divisive normalization across its hierarchy. In a two-stage instantiation (V1 ↔ V2), increasing feedback from V2 to V1 amplifies responses in both areas. We analytically derive power spectra (V1) and coherence spectra (V1-V2) as functions of frequency (f ) and compare them with experimental observations: peaks in both spectra shift to higher frequencies with increased stimulus contrast, and power decays as 1/f 4 at high frequencies. The closed-form spectra are validated against direct stochastic simulation of the full nonlinear circuit across contrasts. The theory further predicts distinctive spectral signatures of feedback and input gain modulation. Crucially, the theory offers a unified view of inter-areal communication, defined as the ability to linearly predict neural activity in one brain area from neural activity in another, with emergent features consistent with empirical observations of both communication subspaces and inter-areal coherence. It admits a low-dimensional communication subspace, where inter-areal communication is lower-dimensional than within-area communication. It further predicts that: (1) increasing feedback strength enhances inter-areal communication and diminishes within-area communication, without altering the subspace dimensionality; (2) communication is strongest, and the subspace dimensionality lowest, at the frequencies at which V1-V2 coherence peaks; (3) normalization reduces the subspace dimensionality. Finally, a three-area (V1 ↔ V4 and V1 ↔ V5) instantiation of the theory demonstrates that differential feedback from higher to lower cortical areas dictates their dynamic functional connectivity. Altogether, our theory provides a robust and analytically tractable framework for generating experimentally testable predictions about normalization, inter-areal communication, and functional connectivity.

item.title: Intervening contexts reshape hippocampal-cortical retrieval states and later source attribution.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Memories are often reactivated in one context and only later judged with respect to where they originally occurred. We tested how an intervening retrieval context shapes neural representations and later source memory. In two fMRI tasks, participants (both male and female) encoded objects within contextual backgrounds, completed an immediate retrieval test in which object cues appeared against either the original background or a different background, and subsequently judged each object's original context on a neutral screen. Shifted cueing contexts reduced source accuracy and biased errors toward the intervening context, despite no detectable difference in immediate recognition or associative-memory performance. Representational similarity analyses showed that encoding patterns reflected original-context structure, whereas immediate-cue-period patterns were broadly organized by the cued (i.e., currently visible) context. On shifted trials, activity patterns showed greater similarity to encoding-derived templates for the cued context than for the original context. Across participants, greater differentiation of original-context similarity between consistent and shifted cueing in posterior hippocampus, parahippocampal cortex, and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex was associated with better source memory after a contextual shift. Within participants, precuneus contextual engagement and dorsal anterior cingulate context alignment predicted later source choices, with similar relationships after adjustment for immediate recognition responses. Later source attribution therefore depended on the contextual state expressed when an item was re-encountered, not simply on reinstatement of the original event.Significance statement Remembering is often described as bringing up the past, but memories are frequently reactivated in new contexts before we judge where they came from. We show that this intervening context can bias later source attribution even when that context is no longer visible at final test. Using two fMRI tasks, representational similarity analysis and trial-level source-choice models, we found that cue-period activity was organized by the context present during cueing and that specific context-state signals predicted later memory choices, whereas item reinstatement did not. Source-memory errors can therefore reflect contextual information encountered after the original event, not only failures to recover the original context.

item.title: Multidimensional dynamics of object representations in the human visual system.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Natural image representations are distributed across many dimensions of visual cortex activity, but little is known about how the multidimensional structure of these representations evolves over time following stimulus onset. Herewe examined the temporal dynamics and latent dimensional structure of natural object representations in large-scale EEG and MEG data from male and female human participants. We also compared these datawith leading representational models derived from large-scale human similarity judgments and deep neural networks. Our findings reveal a rapid expansion of stimulus dimensionality in the brain, which peaks within 100 milliseconds and gradually decays over hundreds of milliseconds. The dynamics of these dimensionality changes tracked the decoding accuracy for both behavioral embeddings and neural network features, suggesting that dimensionality may be a general indicator of representational expressivity. Interestingly, the dimensionality of the neural representations could not be fully explained by a leading behavior-based model or deep neural network. Follow-up experiments showed that the remaining neural variance carried additional perceptually relevant information not yet explained by leading models. Together, these findings reveal previously unrecognized complexity in measurements of dynamic human brain responses to natural objects.Significance Statement When we look at an object, our brains rapidly construct a rich internal representation of what we see. Using large-scale, time-resolved brain recordings from people viewing thousands of natural images, we find that the brain rapidly expands its representational complexity within the first 100 milliseconds, sustaining this richness for hundreds of milliseconds thereafter. A leading behavioral model and a large-scale deep neural network do not fully account for this complexity - yet the unexplained brain activity is not noise: people can reliably use these residual neural patterns to judge image similarity. These findings challenge the assumption that such brain recordings are informationally limited and reveal structure in the human visual system that future models will need to explain.

item.title: Connectome fingerprinting predicts prefrontal cortical activation during abstract reasoning.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Connectome fingerprinting (CF) is a machine-learning technique that uses an individual's unique brain connectivity profile to make predictions about their individual brain activity patterns. Previous studies have successfully employed CF using sensory, working memory, and auditory/visual functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) data. Here, we demonstrate that this technique can be used to examine higher-order cognition and evaluate the effectiveness of the CF method in the prefrontal cortex (PFC), an area where brain function and structure has been shown to be exceptionally variable across individuals. We designed a CF model, using a leave-one-out cross-validation scheme, to predict individually-specific blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) activation in the lateral PFC. We used an abstract reasoning task designed to probe higher-order cognitive function specific to the lateral PFC. Our results demonstrated that CF better predicts abstract reasoning activation in the lateral PFC compared to the group average. We also tested whether task-evoked BOLD activity could be predicted using a model trained on a subset of the functional connectome. We demonstrate that CF models trained on a partial connectome from associative brain networks achieved similar levels of model performance compared to models trained on the full connectome. We observed that model performance varied across participants, suggesting that within-participant reliability in task activation, and deviation from the group average influence the model. Overall, we used CF to characterize individuals' task-evoked BOLD activation during abstract reasoning, demonstrating a link between resting-state functional architecture and brain activations and identifying key networks that contribute to higher-order cognition.

item.title: Posterior alpha/beta oscillations reflect oculomotor dynamics underlying subsequent memory effects.
item.description:
Nature communications
Neural activity and eye movements are well-established predictors of human memory performance. Successful memory formation is associated with reduced alpha/beta power and increased eye movements. However, their coupling and combined contribution to memory formation remain largely unknown. Across four experiments combining eye tracking with scalp or intracranial electroencephalography during free or constrained viewing, we identify the degree of visual exploration, rather than subsequent memory performance, as consistent modulator of posterior alpha/beta power. Going beyond correlations, manipulating eye movements dissociated alpha/beta power reductions from memory. Together with the finding that saccade parameters predicted alpha/beta dynamics, our results directly link posterior alpha/beta activity to the oculomotor system. Moreover, the accumulation of saccades over time accounted for reduced alpha/beta power, resembling the canonical post-stimulus alpha/beta pattern. Our work demonstrates that posterior alpha/beta activity strongly reflects eye movements, supporting alternative perspectives on alpha/beta subsequent memory effects and the general function of posterior alpha/beta activity.

item.title: Beyond memory strengthening: noradrenergic control of memory specificity.
item.description:
Trends in neurosciences
Emotionally significant events are typically remembered better and for longer than mundane experiences. This emotional memory enhancement critically depends on arousal-induced norepinephrine release within the brain. Beyond memory strengthening, recent work shows that noradrenergic activity also shapes the specificity, detailedness, and temporal precision of memories during both early consolidation and systems consolidation. In this review, we synthesize recent findings from human and animal research spanning molecular, circuit, systems, and behavioral mechanisms to propose an integrative framework for how emotional arousal-induced noradrenergic activity affects neural systems that regulate memory specificity and systems consolidation dynamics. The proposed framework refines current models of memory under emotional arousal and may have relevant implications for stress-related psychopathologies.

item.title: A theory of generalized vector coding and subicular function.
item.description:
Current biology : CB
Neural information processing is inextricably linked to the selectivity of individual neurons, as described by their receptive fields. Far from the sensory periphery, neural representations are the result of substantial upstream processing, mixed with internally generated information. Low-dimensional spatial codes in the hippocampal formation offer a handle on understanding these representations. The subiculum, a key but comparatively understudied hippocampal area, exhibits numerous, seemingly unrelated neural codes. Neurons like boundary vector cells, corner cells, or axis-tuned cells are named after the environmental features that appear to drive them, but a common account for their neuronal selectivity is lacking. Here, we propose Disco, a theory explaining subicular functions and related neural codes in other areas. Given the continuous flow of experience, subicular activity can be understood as signaling discontinuities in that flow, coded in a vector base. Geometric discontinuities drive responses to walls, drops, objects, holes, corners, and curved surfaces. The generality of Disco enables predictions for 3D environments, natural scenes, and mixed-modality coding. Discontinuities are not identical to the concept of boundaries (abstract or spatial), as illustrated by non-spatial discontinuities in behavioral state. These yield axis coding in the model (activity along parallel maze arms). Finally, tracking population activity signals event boundaries as discontinuities in neural space. The emergence of diverse neural activity suggests that discontinuity coding may serve as a key principle in the subiculum and related brain areas supporting (spatial) memory and navigation.

item.title: Age-related changes in brain connectivity: Cross-sectional and longitudinal effects.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Age-related changes in functional connectivity within and between brain networks may contribute to cognitive and behavioral decline in aging. Prior research has consistently reported declines in within-network connectivity with age, though findings on between-network connectivity change have been mixed. Most studies have relied on cross-sectional designs, making it difficult to disentangle age-related effects from confounding cohort effects. Therefore, this study utilizes both cross-sectional (between-subject) and longitudinal (within-subject) datasets and employs mixed-effects models to elucidate age-related changes in resting-state functional connectivity across eight large-scale brain networks. After clinical screening and motion-based quality control, analyses were based on resting-state fMRI from 53 younger adults and 127 older adults, 45 of whom were rescanned approximately 4 years later. We examined whole-brain within-network connectivity, between-network connectivity, and network segregation. Cross-sectionally, older age was associated with lower within-network (p < 0.001) and between-network connectivity (p = 0.003), whereas segregation showed a more modest cross-sectional reduction that was concentrated in the salience and visual networks. Longitudinally, over approximately 4 years both within-network (p = 0.003) and between-network (p = 0.003) connectivity declined, while segregation did not change (p = 0.546). Declines in within- and between-network connectivity were broad rather than network specific, with the Default Mode and Salience networks most consistently affected.

item.title: Hierarchical coding of local and global positions in episodic memory for naturalistic sequences.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Life unfolds continuously across multiple timescales, yet how the brain encodes hierarchical event sequences remains poorly understood. Using magnetoencephalography, we investigated the neural coding of hierarchical positions in naturalistic sequence memory. Participants viewed video sequences with a nested structure and later recalled their serial order. Behavioral analyses revealed transposition errors for items occupying identical global or local position. Multivariate classification and subspace analyses revealed separable neural representations of global and local positions. Local positions were better decoded in sensor space, whereas global positions exhibited greater pattern separability in neural subspace. Brain regions encoding global positions exhibited longer neural timescales, reduced sensitivity to low-level event transitions, and stronger representation for high-level event content, compared to regions encoding local positions. These findings motivate a parallel hierarchical organization of content and context, a novel framework that enables integration of item and order across hierarchical levels and provides principles for hierarchical sequence representation in the brain.

item.title: Transferring active inference to newly encountered prism-shifted environments.
item.description:
Communications biology
Rapid adaptability to sudden changes in environmental contingencies is a hallmark of biological intelligence. However, how animals flexibly adapt to novel environments remains largely unclear. To investigate the brain's generalizability, this work focuses on prism adaptation, a classical visuomotor phenomenon reflecting rapid recalibration of perception-action coupling. Modeling is conducted based on canonical neural networks that instantiate active inference at the circuit level. Namely, we develop canonical neural networks equipped with multiple policy matrices in parallel, enabling the reuse of previously acquired sensorimotor knowledge. We demonstrate that the proposed model recapitulates key features of prism adaptation in an arm-reaching task, including rapid error reduction and after-effects following prism removal. Networks employing policies pretrained for different target positions adapt substantially faster than naive networks that relearn policies from scratch. These results suggest a biologically plausible mechanism by which neural circuits flexibly reuse prior knowledge to support rapid adaptation.

item.title: Causal role of human hippocampus in relational structure learning and inference.
item.description:
Nature human behaviour
When meeting new individuals or known individuals in new circumstances, we intuitively map out their relationships-not merely through direct experience, but by inferring new connections on the basis of prior relational knowledge. How such relational knowledge is represented and used in the brain remains a long-standing question in cognitive neuroscience. Here, using a behavioural task and computational modelling, we show that participants (N = 36) leveraged existing knowledge of relational structures to infer new relationships, facilitating adaptation in changing environments. Whole-brain neuroimaging identified consistent representations of relational structure in the hippocampus. To investigate the causal link between hippocampal representations and inference, we used neural network simulations to predict the behavioural effects of disrupting such representations. Consistent with this prediction, transcranial ultrasound stimulation of the human hippocampus (N = 20), transiently modulating its activity, disrupted structure-based inference (P < 0.001, Cohen's d = -0.89, 95% confidence interval -1.41 to -0.36), providing empirical evidence for a causal role of hippocampus in relational-structure learning and structure-based inference.

item.title: From Variability to Synchrony: Non-linear Development of Auditory Neural Responses During the First Year of Life.
item.description:
NeuroImage
In humans, the first year of life is characterized by rapid developmental changes, including substantial brain maturation. As a result, neural responses to auditory stimuli undergo marked changes during this period. In this study, we followed 69 infants across their first year of life and recorded high-density electroencephalography (hdEEG) at 2 weeks, 6 months, and 12 months postpartum. Infants were presented with pure beep tones to examine the development of neural responses to auditory stimulation. We analyzed event-related potentials (ERPs), inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC), and event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP) responses to the beep tones and controlled for arousal state during stimulus presentation. We found that with increasing age, neural responses became more pronounced and showed reduced trial-to-trial variability. Phase synchronization increased from 2 weeks to later developmental stages in a broad low-frequency range (0.5 Hz to 13.6 Hz), indicating improved temporal alignment of brain responses over time. However, phase synchronization decreased from 6 to 12 months, suggesting a developmental transition towards more differentiated brain activity. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that auditory maturation during the first year of life follows a non-linear trajectory driven by dynamic changes in neural synchronization, reflecting the progressive refinement of functional neural circuits. Our results thus provide a critical benchmark for understanding the neural dynamics underlying sensory development during this period.

item.title: Multidimensional psycholinguistic difficulty in Cantonese picture naming: Behavioral, neural, and effective connectivity evidence.
item.description:
Brain and language
Picture naming is a useful paradigm for studying spoken word production because it requires the transformation of visual object input into a lexical response through coordinated conceptual and lexical processes. This study examined whether inherent psycholinguistic difficulty in picture naming is multidimensional or unitary. Thirty-eight healthy native Cantonese speakers performed an overt object picture-naming task during fMRI. Four psycholinguistic variables were modeled: conceptual familiarity, average neighborhood distance (AND), naming disagreement, and lexical frequency. Mixed-effects models showed that higher conceptual familiarity and lexical frequency facilitated naming, whereas higher AND increased both errors and response times; naming disagreement increased errors but did not significantly affect response times. Importantly, we observed a significant interaction between conceptual familiarity and lexical frequency on response times, indicating the facilitative effect of frequency was modulated by familiarity. For errors, significant interactions were found between conceptual familiarity and lexical frequency, as well as between AND and lexical frequency, and between AND and naming disagreement, revealing complex joint influences on naming accuracy. Whole-brain analyses revealed dissociable neural effects across variables. Conjunction analysis showed that lower conceptual familiarity and higher AND converged in bilateral lateral occipital and ventral occipitotemporal regions, with extension into the left posterior temporal cortex, suggesting shared sensitivity to semantic-level difficulty. In contrast, naming disagreement and lexical frequency did not show significant lexical-level overlap. Effective connectivity analyses further identified a stable directed ROI architecture during naming. Together, the findings support a multidimensional account of picture-naming difficulty in which semantic- and lexical-related item properties impose partially distinct but interacting constraints on spoken word production.

item.title: Spatial and functional organization of the somato-cognitive action network (SCAN) during cue and execution of motor tasks.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
The primary motor cortex has traditionally been conceptualized as a somatotopically organized structure, with discrete cortical regions corresponding to specific body parts. However, accumulating evidence suggests that motor cortex organization extends beyond simple effector-based representations to include higher-order functional systems supporting goal-directed behavior. Here, we examine the somato-cognitive action network (SCAN), a set of inter-effector cortical regions located between the classical hand, foot, and face representations of primary motor cortex that has been proposed to integrate cognitive control processes with motor function. Using task-based functional MRI during a motor paradigm that dissociates cue-related and execution-related processes, we investigated the functional role and spatial organization of SCAN in healthy adults. SCAN exhibited preferential activation during the cue phase, greater than during movement execution, indicating a prominent role in action preparation rather than motor output. In contrast, classical effector-specific motor representations corresponding to individual body parts (hand, foot, and face) showed greater engagement during execution, consistent with their role in movement generation. Across these SCAN regions, activation increased systematically from dorsomedial regions (adjacent to leg representations) to ventrolateral regions (adjacent to face representations). This spatial gradient was accompanied by progressively greater dominance of preparatory SCAN activity relative to movement-related activity in the adjacent effector regions. Together, these findings demonstrate that motor cortex organization includes a distinct integrative system that is temporally and spatially dissociable from effector-specific representations. These results support an integrate-isolate framework in which cognitive and motor processes are differentially expressed across the cortical landscape, providing new insight into the functional architecture of human motor control.

item.title: Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns of Dynamic Audiovisual Social Stimuli in Autism Spectrum Disorder (Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns in Autism).
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
The neural basis of social difficulties in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) remains uncertain. Prior studies typically used static stimuli or reduced complex stimuli to only a few dimensions, obscuring real-world complexity. Here, we used videos with social content to engage brain networks and trained encoding models to predict brain activity from high-dimensional audio, visual, and more abstract socially relevant features (e.g., valence). We hypothesized that brain activity in autistic adults would be less accurately predicted and more heterogeneous within and across individuals than in neurotypical (NT) participants, particularly for socially relevant features. Participants [48 ASD (13 female), 90 NT (25 female)] viewed six videos (5-20 min). Brain activity was measured using fMRI. Cross-validated encoding models were assessed on prediction accuracy, variance, and pattern similarity. Brain activity was predicted significantly above chance across brain networks and videos with striking consistency between groups. Auditory and language networks were most accurately predicted. Within-participant predictions were equally variable between groups; however, autistic participants exhibited lower within-group encoding pattern similarity than NT participants and greater across-group than within-group similarity. Analyses using only socially relevant features showed the largest across-group differences in encoding pattern similarity. The novel application of encoding models to multiple videos in ASD suggests greater heterogeneity in neural representations of social information in ASD. Although group-averaged encoding accuracies were comparable across groups, ASD participants showed more heterogeneous regional encoding patterns. These idiosyncratic patterns underscore the need to incorporate individual variation in brain representations when developing translational neuroimaging approaches in autism.Significance statement Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) experience difficulties in social communication and interaction, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we present a novel application of encoding models to neuroimaging in ASD. Neural representations of dynamic and complex social information were more heterogeneous across autistic as compared with neurotypical individuals while encoding model prediction accuracy was similar for population averages across groups. Effects were robust across six videos and spatial scales. Variability in neural representation across individuals, rather than systemic population differences, may thus be associated with atypical brain function in complex social information processing in autism. The findings highlight the importance of accounting for individual variability when studying the neurobiology of autism and developing translational neuroimaging approaches.

item.title: The disrupted navigational compass: pathophysiological mechanisms and clinical interventions for spatial navigation deficits.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Spatial navigation is a higher-order integrative cognitive ability that supports environmental orientation, goal-directed route selection, and adaptive locomotion by integrating spatial memory, multisensory cues, attention, and executive control. Neural systems supporting navigation are also vulnerable to aging and neurodegenerative disease, making navigation a useful domain for linking basic mechanisms with clinically measurable functional impairment. This review summarizes spatial-navigation mechanisms across multiple levels. At the cognitive level, navigation depends on interacting processes including spatial representation, path integration, reference-frame transformation, landmark use, and route planning. At the network level, hippocampal-entorhinal, retrosplenial-parietal, scene-selective, and prefrontal systems contribute complementary functions. At the cellular level, place-, grid-, head-direction-, speed-, and boundary-related representations encode position, heading, self-motion, environmental geometry, and prospective behavior. Clinical and neuroimaging studies indicate that navigation impairment is associated with structural and functional abnormalities, with the strongest diagnostic evidence currently arising from Alzheimer's disease and its prodromal stages. VR-based behavioral assessment and electrophysiological approaches provide complementary means of characterizing navigation phenotypes: VR enables controlled, repeatable, process-sensitive tasks, whereas intracranial and scalp recordings provide neural information at different spatial and physiological scales. No pharmacological agent has been developed or licensed specifically for navigation impairment; current navigation-focused interventions therefore rely mainly on behavioral and VR-based rehabilitation, compensatory strategies, and emerging neuromodulation approaches. Future studies should integrate process-specific behavioral and physiological markers with biomarker-defined clinical cohorts, and use large, randomized, longitudinal studies to establish diagnostic validity, real-world transfer, and mechanism-informed intervention effects.

item.title: Multidimensional neural maturity indices from naturalistic fMRI reveal the longitudinal development of theory of mind.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Theory of Mind (ToM) develops from early reasoning about others' beliefs and intentions toward more advanced forms of recursive and socially embedded mental-state understanding. This ability emerges alongside the progressive maturation of large-scale brain networks. Here, we introduce a multidimensional neural maturity framework, derived from naturalistic functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), that characterizes children's neurofunctional maturation along three dimensions: functional connectivity, temporal fluctuation, and spatial activation, by capturing neural responses to social narratives. Using an accelerated longitudinal design (baseline ages 3-9 years; 27-30-month follow-up), we applied this framework to examine how social-cognitive brain networks mature across complementary dimensions of brain function and how such maturation relates to ToM development. Across childhood, all three neural indices increased longitudinally, indicating progressive maturation of social-cognitive networks. Brain-behavior analyses further highlighted temporal fluctuation and spatial activation maturity as dimensions most closely related to ToM performance. Longitudinal path models indicated developmental continuity from elementary to advanced ToM, and suggested that advanced mental-state reasoning develops in coordination with the multidimensional longitudinal maturation of social-cognitive neural responses. Together, these findings provide initial longitudinal neurodevelopmental evidence that children's social-cognitive networks become increasingly adult-like across multiple neurofunctional dimension, offering a neurodevelopmental extension of behavioral accounts of the transition from elementary to advanced mental-state reasoning.

item.title: Associations between white matter network alterations and visuospatial and social-emotional deficits in patients with right hemisphere tumors: a prospective clinico-radiological study.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Preserving neurological function is crucial in brain tumor surgery. Because the right hemisphere supports visuospatial and social‑cognitive abilities, damage may affect quality of life. This prospective study (TANGO; ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04288505) examined associations between visuospatial and social‑emotional deficits and tractography‑based white matter alterations in patients with right hemisphere tumors. Thirty‑four patients were assessed preoperatively and 22 postoperatively using diffusion magnetic resonance imaging and four neuropsychological tests. Tractography metrics were extracted for nine right hemisphere tracts. Thirty‑four Human Connectome Project participants served as controls. Preoperatively, deficits in visuospatial functioning, facial emotion recognition, and mentalizing were associated with predominantly right hemisphere microstructural abnormalities within distributed white matter networks. Visuospatial deficits were associated with alterations involving the frontal aslant tract (FAT), arcuate fasciculus (AF), superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF), and SLF II; facial emotion recognition deficits with the SLF III and uncinate fasciculus (UF); and mentalizing deficits with the AF. Postoperatively, exploratory findings suggested associations between new social-emotional deficits and structural alterations involving the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF), SLF, and SLF III, whereas new visuospatial deficits showed a trend toward reduced right FAT volume. Relative to controls, left hemisphere tractographic changes were observed regardless of the presence of visuospatial and/or social-emotional deficits, whereas right hemisphere alterations were primarily observed in patients with such deficits. These findings highlight the role of right hemisphere networks in supporting visuospatial and social-emotional functioning. Further characterization of white matter connectivity may help improve risk stratification, surgical planning, and rehabilitation strategies.

item.title: The many facets of human brain asymmetry.
item.description:
Nature reviews. Neuroscience
Asymmetry on the left-right axis is an organizing principle of the human brain that is important for diverse cognitive and behavioural functions. Advances in neuroimage analysis, genomics and large-scale data collection in the past decade have transformed our understanding of the biological foundations and multivariate nature of brain asymmetry. In this Review, we synthesize evidence across scales - from functional and macro-anatomical asymmetries and their inter-relations to microstructural, cellular and molecular levels. We examine inter-individual variation and atypical forms of brain asymmetry, which reveal that diverse aspects of asymmetry can vary largely independently across individuals rather than constituting a single trait. In this context, we discuss the developmental origins, lifespan trajectories and genetic architecture of hemispheric differences. We also summarize the relevance of brain asymmetry for neurological and psychiatric disorders and evolutionary changes of brain asymmetry that occurred in humans. Through this synthesis, we illustrate how contrasting the left and right hemispheres provides an informative window into the multi-level brain organization that supports cognition and behaviour.

item.title: Multidimensional relationship between physical health and the brain, mental health, and cognitive development in the ABCD cohort: A 10-year review and future directions.
item.description:
Developmental cognitive neuroscience
The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study® provides an unprecedented opportunity to examine how physical health, mental health, and neurobiological and neurocognitive developmental trajectories intersect throughout adolescence. Findings to date highlight complex interactions between lifestyle behaviors (e.g., physical activity, screen use, diet, sleep) and cardiometabolic outcomes in relation to neurocognitive development. For example, physical activity and sports participation are linked to enhanced executive functioning and healthier brain morphology, whereas variation in cortical and subcortical structures are associated with obesity and sleep disturbances. Excessive screen use and inadequate sleep further correlate with adverse cardiometabolic profiles and poorer neurocognitive outcomes. These relationships are affected by sociodemographic factors, family and social context, and adverse childhood experiences, which may moderate health behaviors and their relationship to cardiometabolic health and neurocognitive development. For example, dietary patterns vary by sex, socioeconomic status, and race/ethnicity, and signs of poor cardiometabolic health (hypertension, dyslipidemia, and obesity) emerge early, showing disparities across demographic groups. Subsequent alterations in neurobiological pathways may then contribute to the persistence of chronic disease risk in these populations. Additionally, pubertal onset, genetics, and medication use may play a role in neurobiological and neurocognitive trajectories and should be considered when conducting analyses. Together, these findings underscore the bidirectional and potentially cyclical nature of the interaction between physical health, mental health, and neurocognitive development, which are shaped by genetic, biological, and social-environmental factors. Future research leveraging ABCD's longitudinal design will be essential for disentangling causal pathways and informing interventions that promote health equity and optimize adolescent health.

item.title: Personalized Functional Network Mapping Across the Lifespan.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Functional brain networks vary substantially across individuals, yet this variability is obscured by conventional group-average atlases. Personalized functional network mapping addresses this limitation by characterizing individual-specific network organization, including the spatial topography of network territories, boundaries, and variants. Personalized mapping can be applied across large developmental and aging cohorts to study lifespan changes in such organization. Precision functional mapping (PFM), a specialized form of personalized mapping, uses extensive functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data per individual to achieve highly reliable and fine-grained characterization of individual functional organization. Here, we review individual-specific functional network organization from infancy through older adulthood. Evidence across life stages suggests a lifespan trajectory in which individual-specific network organization is detectable near birth, continues to refine through childhood and adolescence, and exhibits marked trait-like stability in adulthood, while its evolution in later life remains less well characterized. Across these stages, inter-individual topographic variability is greater in higher-order association than primary sensorimotor systems, positioning the sensorimotor-association axis as a unifying framework for understanding individual-specific network organization across the lifespan. We further review how individualized network features relate to cognition and psychopathology and how they are altered in psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. Finally, we discuss advances in MRI acquisition and analysis that facilitate personalized functional network mapping and opportunities for precision clinical translation.

item.title: Disentangling the Spatiotemporal Neural Dynamics of Conflict Detection and Resolution between Lexical and Sublexical Processes in Oral Word Reading: An Intracranial SEEG Study.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Object recognition relies on correspondence between whole objects and their subcomponents. When this correspondence is disrupted, accurate recognition requires detecting conflicts and inhibiting misleading subcomponent information, yet the neural basis underlying these processes remain unclear. Written language, with sublexical components that may conflict with whole words, provides an ideal testbed. Using stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) recorded from 39 participants (both sexes) during Chinese character reading, we revealed a functional dissociation between neural systems supporting conflict detection and inhibitory control. Conflict detection was associated with β band activity in the fusiform gyrus and widespread θ and α band effects across temporal and parietal regions. Inhibitory control was associated with α and β band activity in the inferior frontal and precentral gyri. Granger causality analysis showed increased β band connectivity from conflict-processing to inhibitory-control regions under conflict conditions. These findings demonstrate that disruptions of whole-sublexical correspondence engage dissociable neural systems for conflict detection and inhibitory control, implemented through frequency- and region-specific neural oscillations and coordinated via increased information transfer from posterior to frontal regions.Significance Statement Reading often requires resolving conflicts between competing linguistic representations, yet the neural mechanisms that detect such conflicts and resolve them remain poorly understood. Using stereo-electroencephalography with millimeter-scale spatial and millisecond-scale temporal resolution, we dissociated sublexical conflict detection from inhibitory control during Chinese character reading. We show that these processes are supported by distinct low-frequency oscillatory networks and are linked through directed functional interactions. These findings move beyond traditional accounts of sublexical effects by identifying their underlying cognitive components and neural dynamics, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding how cognitive control supports fluent word recognition.

item.title: Category learning drives cortical attentional gain to diagnostic dimensions of perceptual information.
item.description:
PLoS biology
Humans and other animals develop remarkable perceptual and cognitive specializations for identifying, differentiating, and acting on classes of ecologically important signals. This expertise is flexible enough to support diverse perceptual judgments: a voice, for example, simultaneously conveys what a talker says, as well as myriad cues about her identity and state. Expert perception across complex signals thus involves discovering and learning regularities that best inform diverse perceptual judgments, as well as weighting this information flexibly as task demands change. Here, we test whether this process may involve attentional gain. We use two prospective auditory category learning tasks to relate a complex, entirely novel soundscape to four classes of 'alien identity' and two classes of 'alien size.' Identity, but not size, categorization requires discovery and learning of patterned acoustic input situated in one of two simultaneous, non-overlapping frequency bands. This allows us to capitalize on the coarsely segregated, frequency-band-specific channels tiling auditory cortex. We use fMRI to ask whether category-relevant perceptual information present in one frequency band is prioritized relative to simultaneous, uninformative information in the other frequency band. Only among participants expert at alien identity categorization do we observe neural prioritization of the identity-diagnostic frequency band. This prioritization persists even when the diagnostic information becomes irrelevant in the size categorization task. Tellingly, the neural selectivity evoked implicitly in the identity categorization task aligns with that in an independent task, where activation is driven by explicit and sustained selective attention to pure tones in one or the other frequency band. Additionally, the learning trajectories taken to achieve expert-level categorization leave fingerprints on the patterns of neural activity associated with the diagnostic dimension. In all, this indicates that learning categories can drive attentional gain to category-diagnostic input dimensions.
